Randall Parrish published this sea novel in 1918, setting it in the days of the early American colonies. Its narrator, Geoffry Carlyle, is a seaman who tells his own story in the first person, looking back on youth, danger, and a woman he never forgot. The tale moves from English jails and forced labor to ships off Virginia and the Chesapeake.

Carlyle is sent into servitude, held on a prison ship, and then drawn aboard the pirate craft Namur, where Dorothy Fairfax is also at risk. Mutiny, murder, escape in an open boat, a slaver, and a hunt for treasure follow, chapter by chapter. Readers get a fast, old-style adventure of loyalty, daring, and love at sea.

Ancient India's sacred law book, the Manava Dharma-sastra, is introduced here under its English name, the Laws of Manu. Brahmins revere it highly and credit it with divine origin and remote antiquity. Its reputed author, Manu, survived the Flood as father of humanity and now enjoys in heaven the rank of an all-knowing deity.

Ten great sages approached Manu and asked him to declare the sacred laws of the castes. He answered by having Bhrigu, carefully taught in the metrical institutes, deliver the instruction. So the work claims to be Manu's dictation through Bhrigu, learned in turn from self-existent Brahma. Contents, castes, duties, and penalties follow in outline.
